The Estate · Neo-Georgian

Then the house appears.

Flemish bond brick. White portico. A circular lawn held before the entrance like a pause.

Garran Hill · 1916

The door has been open
since 1916.

Leonard Tufts' craftsmen built it. The same men who built Pinehurst.

Seven fireplaces. Four columns. Original 1916 brick.
4.15 acres. 6,072 square feet.

It has not been divided. It has not been converted. It has not been asked to be something else.

Walter Hines Page · László portrait · London, 1917

The History · Walter Hines Page

He named it Garran Hill.
He never spent a night here.

He bought the land in February 1913. Named it Garran Hill. Six weeks later, Woodrow Wilson appointed him Ambassador to the Court of St. James.

He sailed for London. Into the war.

The house was completed without him. His son Ralph supervised. Leonard Tufts' craftsmen built it. From London, through four years, he wrote home about one thing.

"The farm — the farm — the farm."

The Life and Letters of Walter H. Page · Vol. I, P. 354 · 1923

He came home in December 1918. Carried from the train at Aberdeen — miles from his land. He died ten days later.

He co-founded Doubleday, Page & Co. He edited The Atlantic Monthly. He nominated Woodrow Wilson for the presidency.

He never spent a night here.

"Well, Frank, I did get here
after all, didn't I?"
Walter Hines Page  ·  Aberdeen, NC  ·  December 1918
He died ten days later.

The Kitchen

The kitchen was not updated.
It was designed.

Reclaimed heart-pine floors — the only room that departs from the original oak.

White cabinetry. Dark granite. Island. Four windows.

The wall of windows faces an expanse of grass bordered by elder magnolias.

Every morning at 6:30, the deer come through.

The shell cabinets are original. The kitchen is not. Both are right.

The Primary Suite

Custom wall panels. A fireplace.
Shower walls drawn at full tile detail.

Fifteen architectural drawings document the decisions Thomas O'Shea made in this room alone. They survive. They transfer with the property.

The primary balcony — 24 by 11 feet — faces the grounds.

Fuchsia chinoiserie.
Tennessee marble.

4.15 Acres · Private Grounds

The world outside these gates
does not exist here.

Twenty-eight irrigation zones. 130-foot well. Underground utilities throughout.

A 20-by-40 salt water pool, surrounded by a brick wall with iron gates. Restored 2022.

The Wee Cottage — complete, self-contained — moved to the grounds by sky crane.

In 1916, those were saplings.
Now they are a forest.

Someone still puts flowers there.
Blue Fox  ·  Betty Dumaine's Irish Hunter  ·  Buried on the grounds

1959 – 1984

Some places remember
who loved them.

Elizabeth Dumaine purchased the property in 1959. She was a foxhunter. She added stables, kennels, and an enclosure for peacocks — known to be guard birds. She changed the name to Hollycrest.

Her favorite horse is buried on the grounds.

Blue Fox. Someone still puts flowers there.

The Restoration · 1999–2001

Beauty was not enough.
The house needed discipline.

In 1999, Thomas O'Shea drew the house from scratch. Every room measured. Every cornice profiled. Every proportion committed to paper before a single board was replaced.

Contractor Dennis Dunagan spent three years executing those drawings.

All seven carved mantels saved. Original oak flooring lifted, repaired, relaid. Period-accurate portico brick — three months to source. Custom Marvin windows made to the 1916 profile.

What stands today is what was designed.

It does not feel added.
It feels inevitable.

National Register · Criterion B

Every claim is sourced.
Every fact is verified.

The Pines Preservation Guild visited April 2024. The property qualifies under Criterion B — significant association with a figure of national importance.

A preservation easement is available. North Carolina tax credit: 25% of fair market value, up to $500,000.
